proposal.title: Load the authoring contract in layers, not all at once
proposal.description: Every time an agent opens this tool it reads the whole contract — the guide, all nine block specs and the full JSON Schema — before writing a single line. That is 52KB, and three quarters of it describes blocks the document will never contain. This proposes printing a short guide plus a catalog of what exists, and letting the agent fetch the spec for the two or three blocks it actually uses.

sections.title: Split `author` into three layers
sections.summary: A typical authoring pass drops from ~52KB to ~9KB.

blocks.text: `author` stays the one command an agent runs first, but it now prints only what is always needed: the rules, the document shape, and a one-line catalog of the blocks available. The detail moves behind flags the agent calls when it knows what it is writing.

cells: one block's guidance, example and schema
the full JSON Schema, on its own

blocks.title: The trade
blocks.text: One or two extra CLI calls per document, in exchange for roughly 11k fewer tokens of context. `validate` already names every problem by path, so the schema does not have to be in front of the agent for it to author.

sections.title: Every block declares a one-line summary
sections.summary: `BlockDef` gains `summary`; the catalog is generated from the registry.

blocks.text: The catalog has to be derived, not hand-written, or it drifts the first time someone adds a block. Each block module already owns its schema, its cross-field check and its guide — the summary joins them there.

sections.title: What stays in the first layer
sections.summary: Whether the agent still gets a schema before it starts writing.

blocks.text: The document envelope — sections, questions, dialog, history, response — is 18KB of schema on its own. The prose already describes the shape an agent has to author. The question is whether dropping it makes authoring self-sufficient or merely cheap.

fields.label: Does `author` include an envelope schema?
fields.description: Both options print the same prose and catalog. The difference is whether the agent can author a valid document without a `validate` round-trip to correct it.

sides.label: Prose only
sides.note: Smallest first load. Mistakes surface as a validate failure with an exact path, one round-trip later.

sides.label: Trimmed schema
sides.note: Roughly doubles the first load, and covers only the parts the agent authors — it never writes the response region.

sections.title: The skill runbook gains a step
sections.summary: Both faces: fetch the contract, then fetch the specs for the blocks you will use.

blocks.text: The skill is a runbook, not a copy of the contract, so it only needs to say when to fetch what. An already-installed old skill keeps working: it runs `author`, and the new output itself tells it to fetch block specs.

blocks.patch:
@@ -95,8 +95,11 @@ function proposalBody(run, buildNote) {
-1. **Contract:** run `author` — the authoring guide + JSON schema
-   for the installed version. It carries the rules, the writing guidance,
-   and every block's spec.
+1. **Contract:** run `author` — the authoring guide for the installed
+   version: the rules, the writing guidance, and a catalog of the blocks.
+2. **Block specs:** pick the blocks this proposal needs, then run
+   `author --block <type>,<type>` for their fields, examples and schema.
+   Fetch only the ones you will use; never author a block from memory.

blocks.title: The failure mode to watch
blocks.text: An agent that reads the catalog and writes a block from memory instead of fetching its spec. The strict schema turns that into a validate failure rather than a bad page, but it costs a round-trip.

sections.title: Where this sits in the tool
sections.summary: Only the CLI's `author` face changes; the file contract is untouched.

blocks.title: Nothing else moves
blocks.text: The document format, the version and the round-trip are unchanged. A proposal written before this change still validates and still opens.

questions.prompt: The document format does not change — bumping the version would reject in-flight files. Bump anyway?

Bump to 0.9.0 — the CLI surface changed

questions.prompt: Is one line per block enough for an agent to pick the right block, or should the catalog also say what each one costs to fetch?
